item.title: Americans don’t have to choose between our AI future and ripping off copyright owners
item.description: The DOJ's embrace of fair use for AI training breaks with the White House's own framework, as OpenAI, Microsoft and news groups battle over copyright.
item.content:encoded:
One of the biggest court battles over artificial intelligence (AI) is putting an age-old legal principle to the test — and raising important questions about the Trump administration's AI policy.

Several news organizations, including The New York Times, are suing OpenAI and Microsoft for using millions of newspaper articles to train AI systems. The newspapers argue that the tech firms violated basic copyright protections. The tech firms contend that training their models on those articles qualifies as "fair use," a longstanding principle that allows copyrighted material to be used in certain ways without permission from or compensation to the copyright owner.

The Department of Justice (DOJ) has sided squarely with OpenAI's position — breaking with the administration's previously more balanced stance on the issue. The DOJ filed a statement of interest embracing an extreme vision of fair use that would grant AI companies virtually unfettered access to copyrighted material for commercial training, without obtaining permission from or compensating the creators whose works fuel these systems.

MIKE DAVIS: THE TRUMP DOJ SHOULD WITHDRAW ITS STATEMENT OF INTEREST IN THE OPENAI LAWSUIT

This expansive interpretation threatens to turn a narrow copyright exception into a blanket exemption for the world's most powerful and profitable industries.

The DOJ's reasoning is that requiring a copyright license for material used in AI training would impose high costs on AI developers. It claims those costs could make it harder for small companies to compete and hamper U.S. AI leadership and national security.

FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS SEE AI REGULATION AS URGENT, RANK SAFEGUARDS AHEAD OF INNOVATION

Those concerns deserve consideration. But the DOJ's aggressive arguments in the brief depart from more measured guidance elsewhere in the administration. The White House's official AI framework acknowledges valid arguments on both sides of the copyright debate.

Likewise, the Carolina Principles for Emerging Technologies, adopted by G20 ministers at the Commerce Department's recent Innovation Ministerial, recognize that the intersection of AI and copyright poses "complex legal and policy questions." The principles note the "essential role" of copyright protections in supporting creators and call for respecting IP as a pillar of G20 AI policy.

MUSIC INDUSTRY FENDS OFF FLOOD OF AI MUSIC 'STEALING' THE CHARTS

The DOJ statement also overlooks how its stance could favor larger AI companies over smaller firms and startups. Several AI startups have argued that paying for the material they use provides more reliable access to training material, reduces legal uncertainty and improves models. Other companies have emerged to aggregate copyrights and make licensing easier.

It's particularly problematic for large AI companies to complain about paying for access to copyrighted materials. They are among the best positioned to pay for those materials, and doing so would help develop the kind of licensing markets they claim are lacking.

OBAMA CRITICIZES TRUMP ON APPROACH TO AI, ESCALATES WARNING FOR STRONGER REGULATION

And even if national security were a legitimate justification, the government could not simply disregard property rights. The Constitution and other laws require just compensation when private property is taken for public use, and intellectual property rights are still property rights. Letting AI firms appropriate creators' IP without permission or compensation would be akin to letting data center builders seize private land without paying fair value.

If courts adopt the DOJ's position that fair use protects AI developers in virtually all circumstances, it would reduce incentives to create new works. Copyrights encourage creative work by assuring writers, artists and other creators that their work can't be easily stolen or copied. Licensing those rights allows creators to earn a living and underpins over $1 trillion in U.S. economic activity.

Weaker copyrights could result in fewer human-created books, articles, research papers, films and songs. Ironically, that could eventually leave AI systems with fewer and lower-quality materials to train on – a scenario that serves no one's interests.

All of this is why the Trump administration would be wise to follow its own AI framework and let the court system evaluate AI copyright disputes case by case, rather than arguing for unfettered fair use exceptions.

Policymakers also have a role to play. One promising bill is the bipartisan CLEAR Act. Introduced in February by California Democrat Sen. Adam Schiff and Utah Republican Sen. John Curtis, the CLEAR Act would require AI developers to publicly disclose the copyrighted works used in each new generative-AI model's training dataset.

The proposal would not settle whether any particular training practice qualifies as fair use. But it would give creators more information about whether their work helped train an AI system, enabling them to pursue appropriate compensation or other remedies when they believe their rights have been violated.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

That kind of targeted reform offers a useful model for copyright enforcement in the age of AI. Rather than treating licensing as an obstacle to innovation, policymakers should foster a market where AI developers can efficiently license copyrighted material while respecting creators' rights.

AI innovation is vital to America's future. But America's creative industries still depend on strong copyright protections. Policymakers need to promote both.

item.title: Republicans face 'brutal' 2028 Senate map after Dems 2026 blue wave
item.description: Incoming NRSC chair Sen. Bernie Moreno calls the GOP's 2028 Senate map "absolutely brutal" as Republicans must flip six seats to reclaim majority control.
item.content:encoded:
Incoming Senate Republican campaign chairman says the party faces a "very tough" road ahead as the GOP aims to take back their majority in 2028 after taking significant losses in the midterms earlier this month.

Democrats convincingly grabbed control of the Senate and will hold a large 56-44 majority when the new Congress is sworn in at the start of the new year, they also won control of the House and multiple governors' seats flip from red to blue, as well.

In the Senate, the new split means Republicans will need to flip at least six seats in the 2028 elections to win back the majority. That number rises to seven seats if they lose the White House in the next election cycle.

One senator told Fox News Digital that Republicans can "forget 2028."

"It is an absolutely brutal map," Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno, the incoming National Republican Senatorial Committee chair, recently told Fox News Digital, as he pointed to the states up for grabs in 2028.

SENATE REPUBLICANS FEAR 'BRUTAL' 2028 MAP COULD KEEP DEMOCRATS IN POWER FOR YEARS

But the first term senator from Ohio added that in "politics, things change pretty quickly."

He's not kidding.

At the start of the 2026 cycle, the Democrats faced a steep and narrow path to winning back the majority, but by Election Day the party was able to ride a massive blue wave formed by an extremely favorable political climate to flip nine Senate seats .

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, looking ahead to the next election, said in an interview on Fox News' "America Reports, "We can come back — we will."

"I've been there before, and we just have to get out and win the hearts and minds of the American people," he added. "And that means coming up with a compelling economic message, talking about secure streets, secure border, safe streets, and in more money in your pocket. I mean, I think those are the things that the American people care the most about."

Looking ahead to the next two years, when he will be leading the GOP minority in the Senate, Thune said "we now have an opportunity in the minority to draw those bold lines, those contrasts, and make sure that we are delivering a message that connects with the middle of the electorate."

In 2028, Republicans will need to hold onto seats in battlegrounds Wisconsin and North Carolina, where GOP Sens. Ron Johnson and Ted Budd are up for re-election.

Meanwhile, Republicans will work to flip seats held by Democratic Sens. Mark Kelly of Arizona, John Fetterman of Pennsylvania, Raphael Warnock of Georgia, Catherine Cortez Masto of Nevada, and Maggie Hassan of New Hampshire.

Dem flips key Senate seat in battleground North Carolina as Cooper defeats Trump ally

TRUMP GRIP ON GOP FACES MAJOR POST-ELECTION TEST

Fetterman, who has repeatedly visibly broken with his party and seen his poll numbers among Democrats crater, faces all-but-certain primary challenges if he seeks re-election. Meanwhile, Kelly and Warnock are mulling White House runs in 2028.

Senate showdowns will also be held in 2028 in six states that President Donald Trump carried by double-digits two years ago that become key battlegrounds in this year's midterms.

Among them are Ohio, where former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown won a ticket back to the Senate with a five point victory over appointed GOP Sen. Jon Husted. Brown will fill out the final two years of Vice President JD Vance's old Senate term, so he'll face re-election in 2028.

Republicans will be defending seats in four states where Democrats scored Senate flips in this year's midterms. The four seats are held by GOP Sens. Chuck Grassley of Iowa, Jerry Moran of Kansas, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, and Tim Scott of South Carolina,

Massive upset: Andrews downs Trump-backed Graham in ruby-red South Carolina

In Florida, appointed Republican Sen. Ashley Moody narrowly defeated progressive Democratic state Rep. Angie Nixon in a special election. Moody, who is filling out Secretary of State Marco Rubio's old Senate term, will face re-election in two years.

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

Kyle Kondik, managing editor of Sabato’s Crystal Ball at the University of Virginia Center for Politics, which is a leading nonpartisan political handicapper, told Fox News Digital Republicans could win the Senate back by flipping six states in 2028 : Arizona, Georgia, Ohio, Nevada, New Hampshire, and Pennsylvania.

Dems seize the Senate as blue tidal wave crashes deep into Trump country, topples GOP strongholds

"Those are five states Trump won state in 2024," as well as New Hampshire, which then-Vice President Kamala Harris carried by single digits.

"The Democrats just showed that they could win all these double-digit Trump states" in the midterms," Kondik noted. "The Republicans don't have to flip any double-digit Harris states to win the Senate back" in 2028.

Kondik also highlighted that there there will be a Senate special election next November, a year ahead of the 2028 showdowns.

That ballot box contest will be held in Minnesota, where Democratic Sen. Amy Klobuchar is about to step down after winning the state's gubernatorial election. Klobuchar will pick a replacement senator when she steps down, and the state will hold a special contest on Election Day 2027 to choose a successor to fill out the final three years of Klobuchar's current term.

item.title: Swift assurances from officials after wave of nationwide outages raises questions, expert says
item.description: SMET CEO Danny Cooper says ruling out a cyberattack too fast risks missing hackers after the JPMorgan Chase, Microsoft outages and air travel ground stop.
item.content:encoded:
Amid a slew of high-profile disruptions that struck major pillars of American life over the past week, including a nationwide ground stop that halted air travel, banking outages at JPMorgan Chase and other lenders, and a service disruption at Microsoft, officials were quick to reassure the public that nothing nefarious was behind the failures.

During the ground stop, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the homeland and the banking system remained secure, insisting that the disruptions showed no signs of a cyberattack or malicious activity.

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton similarly stated that officials saw no evidence of a coordinated or state-sponsored attack, pointing instead to routine patching and system upgrades.

DHS CHIEF TELLS AMERICANS TO 'BREATHE' AMID TECH OUTAGES, INSISTS HOMELAND IS 'SECURE'

"Based on what we know today … these are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes," Clayton told the House Homeland Security Committee on Wednesday. "They are not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack."

Major companies, including Microsoft and JPMorgan Chase, also attributed the disruptions to internal technical issues or software bugs rather than malicious intrusions.

US INFRASTRUCTURE CRUMBLES AS ADVERSARIES POWER UP – LEAVING AMERICANS DANGEROUSLY EXPOSED: CYBER EXPERT

To Danny Cooper, CEO of critical infrastructure security firm SMET, the speed with which those assurances were issued poses a problem.

"A blanket statement like 'there's no malicious activity associated with any of the outages' is almost impossible from a probability perspective," Cooper told Fox News Digital.

THE OUTAGES AMERICA HAS SUFFERED WEREN'T AN ATTACK, BUT THE NEXT FAILURE COULD BE

Public anxiety tends to spike around a single question in the aftermath of a major disruption: Was it a coincidence or an attack? Public skepticism is understandable given how many critical systems stumbled within a five-to-six-day window, Cooper said.

"How plausible is it that all these pillars or whatever all suffered major independent technical failures within a five- or six-day window?" Cooper asked. "I think highly improbable. And I understand why the American public is calling this into question and deeply empathize with that. The pattern recognition is there."

DUFFY: INVESTIGATORS EXAMINING 2 ROUTERS AFTER NATIONWIDE FAA GROUND STOP, NO SIGNS OF FOREIGN CYBERATTACK

Even when officials point to routine maintenance or aging hardware, Cooper argued that ruling out foul play too quickly skips investigative steps that take time to execute properly, which could potentially undermine efforts to fix vulnerabilities and prevent future incidents.

"If a company or the government is making a statement that is as bold as 'we are certain there is no malicious activity here' without having the time to actually do an appropriate investigation, in the case of this sort of cyber domain, some cyber forensics and a full audit of what transpired, that's not quite how it works," she said.

PERPETUAL PARALYSIS: WHY EVERYTHING IS GRINDING TO A HALT

"On the physical side, being able to fully interrogate what has happened in the environment, who was there, and so on about what is happening in the periphery and what led up to that moment in time, those things take time."

An instant "nothing to see here" message can also deepen public suspicion, Cooper said, particularly when multiple institutions and agencies echo that conclusion before audits can be completed.

JOIN THE CHAT: RECENT TECH OUTAGES LOOM OVER MULLIN TESTIMONY ON WORLDWIDE THREATS

The Democratic National Committee (DNC) also sounded the alarm over conflicting statements coming from the Trump administration.

"The administration has repeatedly offered conflicting statements about the causes of the outages," DNC Deputy Communications Director Kendall Witmer said in a statement. "Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin suggested that SI – Trump’s preferred name for Artificial Intelligence (AI) – is responsible for the multiple outages that have occurred in recent days, according to a "very smart" tech guy he talked to. Then, yesterday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio contradicted Mullin and would not attribute the outages to AI."

MICROSOFT’S MASSIVE OUTAGE OFFERS A LESSON IN HOW TO BRING THE WORLD BACK ONLINE

Much of the official explanation surrounding the November disruptions centered on software updates and system upgrades. Organizations frequently schedule maintenance and can experience downtime when rolling out changes at scale, especially if teams move too quickly, Cooper noted.

However, those windows are what sophisticated adversaries watch closely, she warned.

"If companies are disproportionately moving to execute these sorts of upgrades en masse, then yes, it's possible that you would have a higher number of downtime or outages," she said.

"But it's also quite possible that, particularly given the sophistication of cyber adversaries, whether it's hackers, whether it's non-state entities, whether it's nation-state entities, it's also possible that they are using those software updates or upgrades or patches and in those moments actually injecting malware and exploits and so on."

item.title: DEPROGRAMMED: He lived as a woman for six years, hit ‘rock bottom’ and found Jesus. Then he detransitioned.
item.description: After six years living as a woman, Diego Arellan says pain, rejection and suicidal thoughts led him to become a Christian through his sister's testimony.
item.content:encoded:
This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline at 988 or 800-273-TALK (8255).

Diego Arellan said he had never encountered transgender ideology until he moved to the United States from Peru as a teenager. He said people later encouraged him to transition because of the way he behaved. Ultimately, he lived as a transgender woman for six years before becoming a Christian and detransitioning.

"I started hanging out with a lot of people that were living that lifestyle and that also recommended me to live that lifestyle because [of] the way I acted," Arellan told Fox News Digital.

"I found that out of like this clinic who offer that pretty much transitioning to become your opposite gender. And so, through that process … in my mind it was like, 'I definitely have to do this because this is the right path. Everything that I'm seeing out there, like in social media, or anywhere I go I see, like this is a way you have to go in order for you to feel fulfilled, at least because I always struggle with my identity,'" he continued.

PRISHA MOSLEY: AS A DETRANSITIONER AND MOM, I KNOW WHAT GENDER IDEOLOGY STOLE FROM ME

"I transitioned when I was 18 and a lot of things happened during that season just because I was very immature in that season … I went through a lot [of] gender dysphoria," Arellan said.

He went on to describe what he said were side effects of the hormone pills he took, saying his body was reacting to something that was "not natural."

"[I had] a lot of like, pain on my body and just changes, but I still went through it because I really thought that this was gonna be the path that was gonna make me happy … There was a lot of rejection as well from the people I start[ed] dating … I was lying not only to me, but I was lying to the people out there who thought they were dating any other woman, but in reality, [I] was not," he continued.

WOMAN WHO LIVED AS MAN SAYS SHE GRIEVED ‘UNWANTED BODY PARTS’ AFTER TRANSITION

"There was a lot of confusion, a lot of stress, a lot like just also wanting to kill myself at one point because of all these things I was building and thinking that this was the right path again," Arellan added.

Arellan said he had breast augmentation surgery, a Brazilian butt lift and Botox injections in different areas of his face.

"It was turning into an addiction because it was never enough. Everything I see on my face … I started to hate it because I just kept looking at myself and I look[ed] at the mirror and I look[ed like] I'm a man just having long hair," he said.

"I achieved everything I wanted [and] I still felt so empty and that's where a lot of things changed," Arellan said.

WOMAN WHO UNDERWENT DOUBLE MASTECTOMY AT 14 TELLS SURGEON, 'YOU STOLE MY GIRLHOOD'

According to a research paper by Eric Kaufmann, published on the Social Science Research Network (SSRN), the share of surveyed university students identifying as transgender fell from nearly 7% in 2023 to under 4% in later survey data. The paper also reported a decline of approximately 10 percentage points in the share identifying as non-heterosexual.

Arellan discussed his move to Miami, where he dated "a sugar daddy" and experienced "crazy" things that opened his heart to his sister’s testimony of her experience with Jesus Christ.

"I was [at] rock bottom, I hated myself. I had a lot of money. I did a lot [of] things that were really bad. But my sister — she shared with me her testimony of how she encountered Jesus — and that was it," he said.

Arellan, who now runs an online shop called "D-King merch" selling Christian clothing, offered advice to people reconsidering their gender transitions.

"Following Jesus is not easy. It can be narrow, it can be hard, but it's so worth it," he said.

item.title: Utah mommy blogger Ruby Franke's daughter begs parole board not to let her out of prison: 'she is a monster'
item.description: Shari Franke revealed weekly nightmares of her mother's house as she urged the Utah Board of Pardons and Parole to keep Ruby Franke behind bars.
item.content:encoded:
Shari Franke, the eldest daughter of disgraced Utah parenting blogger and convicted child abuser Ruby Franke, urged the Utah Board of Pardons and Parole to keep her and former associate Jodi Hildebrandt behind bars ahead of their upcoming parole hearings.

Ruby Franke, a mother of six children, and Jodi Hildebrandt ran a joint parenting and lifestyle YouTube channel called ConneXions Classrooms before being arrested and charged with six counts of second-degree aggravated child abuse in a St. George courtroom in December 2023. Both were sentenced in February 2024 to four consecutive prison terms of one to 15 years after pleading guilty to four counts of aggravated child abuse.

Under Utah law, both face between four and 30 years behind bars, with the state's parole board determining their release.

Ruby Franke and Hildebrandt were charged after police rescued two of Franke's malnourished children from Hildebrandt's home on Aug. 30, 2023. The children had endured severe abuse, including forced physical labor, food deprivation, emotional mistreatment and having their hands and feet bound. Franke and Hildebrandt also told the children they were evil and needed to be punished.

MOMMY BLOGGER RUBY FRANKE ASKED DAUGHTER FOR ONE THING BEFORE ARREST: MEMOIR

The abuse came to light after one of Franke's children escaped Hildebrandt's home and sought help from a neighbor, who called police.

In an Instagram post, Shari Franke shared her statement to the Utah Board of Pardons & Parole, where she asked them not to grant her mother and Hildebrandt parole.

Shari Franke said she hasn't spoken to her mother in four years, describing their last conversation as "the most stressful experience of my life." She said Ruby Franke told her she no longer wanted her to be part of the family because she had spoken out against her.

I called the police, I called CPS, I spoke to lawyers. And Ruby and Jodi evaded all of them," Shari Franke said. "I will never accept Ruby’s apology for what she has done. She has been a monster her entire adult life, and there’s no way that’s changed in 3 years."

Shari Franke noted that her mother isn't in prison for what she did to her or her brother growing up, and hasn't yet taken accountability for that. Ruby Franke's daughter said she continues to have nightmares "at least weekly" of being "trapped" back at her mother's house, trying to save her siblings.

item.title: $500M investment could bring AI robots to your workplace
item.description: Genesis AI raised $500 million to expand its general-purpose robot Eno, which learns physical skills from workers wearing special electronic gloves.
item.content:encoded:
What if a robot could learn how to do your job simply by watching you work? That's what Genesis AI is working toward, and some of the biggest names in tech are betting big on it. The robotics company has raised $500 million to bring its general-purpose robot, Eno, into more workplaces. The investment values Genesis at $3.5 billion and puts some serious financial muscle behind its plans.

But what really caught my attention is how these robots learn. Genesis is developing technology that allows people to teach robots physical skills without having to program every movement. Workers wear special electronic gloves while doing their regular jobs. The gloves capture their hand movements and turn that information into training data that helps robots learn to perform similar tasks.

Eventually, Genesis wants these robots to handle complex work without someone constantly supervising them. The company plans to bring Eno to customer sites in 2027, starting with industrial workplaces. So how close are we to robots that can actually do our jobs, and what happens to the people teaching them? Let's take a closer look.

Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.

Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.

AI BUILDS VIRTUAL HOMES WHERE ROBOTS LEARN FROM THEIR MISTAKES

Genesis AI announced a $500 million Series A funding round at a $3.5 billion post-money valuation. Premji Invest, Khosla Ventures and Eclipse co-led the investment. Other backers include NVIDIA, AMD Ventures, Samsung Next and Zoom. Former Google CEO Eric Schmidt, Zoom CEO Eric Yuan and Yahoo co-founder Jerry Yang are also among the investors. T. Rowe Price-advised accounts and several other major financial and technology firms participated. That's a significant vote of confidence in a company developing robots that can perform physical work across different environments.

Genesis plans to use the funding to expand robot training and improve its artificial intelligence. The company is also increasing production of Eno while hiring additional researchers and robotics engineers. "Our mission is to remove the physical limits on human ambition," said Zhou Xian, co-founder and CEO of Genesis AI. The company wants to move beyond robots programmed to repeat a single task. Its larger goal is to build machines that can adapt to changing conditions and eventually handle entire workflows.

Eno takes a different approach from humanoid robots designed to closely resemble people. Genesis has focused on giving the machine useful physical capabilities rather than recreating every aspect of human appearance. The robot combines dexterous hands with a body designed for practical work. Its hands can handle tools and objects that require careful control, while its AI helps it respond to different physical tasks.

At the center of the technology is GENE, the company's AI foundation model, which acts as the robotic brain. The system helps robots interpret their surroundings and control precise physical movements. We previously covered Genesis AI's robotic brain and its ability to perform complex hand movements. Now, the company is working to bring that intelligence into Eno for commercial use. For now, Genesis has demonstrated several advanced skills using a test robot powered by GENE. Those capabilities are expected to move to Eno as development continues.

How does a robot learn to handle delicate objects or perform tasks that require precise finger movements? We asked Genesis AI co-founder and president Théophile Gervet to explain how its electronic gloves make that possible. "The electronic gloves are worn while people are performing their regular work so we can collect massive amounts of real-world data about how humans perform physical tasks in order to train GENE, our robotic brain."

The gloves capture detailed finger movements and the pressure applied when handling different materials. Genesis designed its robotic hands to closely match human hands, creating what the company calls a 1:1:1 mapping between the human hand, glove and robotic hand. "This process enables Eno to learn complex physical skills without having to manually program every movement," Gervet explained.

Genesis also uses small cameras worn on workers' heads to record tasks from their point of view. "This lets GENE see exactly what someone sees as they perform a task, including how they use their hands and interact with their surroundings," Gervet said. The company also trains GENE using existing videos of people performing physical work. Together, these sources help the AI develop more complex physical skills.

Genesis has another training advantage. Its robots can practice inside Genesis World, a simulation platform that recreates physical environments. For example, a robot learning to play the piano can study movements collected from someone wearing the electronic gloves. It can then repeatedly practice those movements inside a virtual environment.

Gervet explained how the training process can speed up learning. "Also, instead of practicing at the piano for an hour or so a day like you and I might, the robot can train in our hyper-realistic simulation, Genesis World, helping it master its task, like playing the piano, much quicker than it would in the real world." That approach allows developers to test movements without relying entirely on expensive physical training sessions.

AUTONOMOUS EXCAVATORS ARE DIGGING WITH EMPTY CABS

Genesis has demonstrated its GENE robotic brain performing several complex activities. These include preparing meals, handling laboratory equipment and assembling wire harnesses. Gervet also cited manipulating a Rubik's Cube as an example of a skill learned through human demonstrations. These activities require precise control of robotic hands.

However, there's an important detail here. These demonstrations currently use a test robot rather than Eno itself. "Today, GENE allows robots to tackle a wide variety of tasks including preparing a meal, lab pipetting, wire harnessing, packaging, and more. These tasks are currently being demonstrated in a test robot and will be exported over to Eno very soon," Gervet told us.

That means Genesis still needs to show how well Eno performs these skills during extended operation in actual workplaces. One investor says the technology has already shown encouraging progress. "What stood out to us was watching Genesis robots complete long, multi-step tasks on their own at the same speed a person would, with smooth and natural movement," said Vedant Agrawal, partner at Premji Invest.

Genesis began proof-of-concept projects and customer pilots in 2026. Now, the company is preparing to bring what it learned into its next phase of commercial deployment. "We started proof of concepts and pilots with customers in 2026 and received valuable insight by working with the customers. Now we are taking these lessons learnt and heading to customer sites in 2027," Gervet told us. The first deployments will focus on manufacturing facilities, logistics operations and laboratories. Genesis has also announced a strategic partnership with LG CNS, LG's consulting and AI transformation business.

The companies plan to evaluate Genesis robots for manufacturing and logistics work at LG operations in the United States. Their partnership could eventually expand to additional industrial customers. Gervet confirmed the relationship and said, "We will share more on our work with them in the coming months." After industrial deployments, Genesis plans to expand into hospitality and healthcare. Home robots and outdoor applications are further down its development roadmap. However, the company has not announced a firm timeline for bringing Eno into people's homes.

As Genesis works toward robots that can handle entire workflows independently, there's an important question about the employees helping train them. Could those same robots eventually take over some of their jobs? We asked Genesis how employees participate in its training program and who owns the data collected through the electronic gloves and cameras. The company says participation is voluntary and that people involved specifically agree to the work. "All employees who participate in data collection have chosen to opt in and have agreed and consented," Genesis told CyberGuy.

The company added that participants understand how the information is collected and that Genesis does not capture personally identifying information. It also says people receive clear information before providing consent. As for ownership, Genesis was direct: "We own the training data that we capture with our gloves and cameras."

That answers an important question about the program. However, the larger issue remains how this technology could eventually affect employment. Workers may voluntarily help train robots today, but those same machines could eventually perform some of their responsibilities without constant human supervision.

Teaching a robot to perform an impressive task under controlled conditions is one thing. Making that same robot work reliably every day inside a busy workplace is another. Industrial environments change constantly. Equipment moves, objects may end up in unexpected locations and people work nearby.

For general-purpose robots to become practical, they need to respond safely when something goes wrong. Genesis believes developing its hardware and AI together will help address those challenges. The company also controls its training systems and simulation technology, allowing engineers to improve different components together. But the biggest unanswered questions involve long-term performance.

Genesis has not provided detailed commercial pricing or independently verified reliability results for Eno across extended customer deployments. Gervet acknowledged the challenge when discussing the future of robotics. "The challenge is making sure these robots can operate reliably and safely in the real world, not just perform impressive demonstrations in controlled environments." Those are exactly the questions businesses will need answered before trusting robots with more responsibility.

You probably won't see an Eno robot rolling into your workplace tomorrow. However, this technology offers an early look at how physical jobs could change over the next several years. If you work in manufacturing or a laboratory, robots like Eno could eventually handle tasks that require constant repetition. That could reduce physically demanding work while changing the skills employers expect from their teams.

For employees, the bigger question is how companies will introduce these machines. Will robots work alongside existing teams, or will businesses eventually use them to reduce staffing? Genesis sees opportunities to make workplaces more productive, but the long-term impact on jobs remains uncertain.

For people outside those industries, the longer-term possibilities include robots that help with household chores or assist in healthcare settings. Those applications remain further away and will require additional safety testing.

HYUNDAI TO SEND 25,000 ATLAS ROBOTS TO THE US

There's something fascinating about the idea of teaching robots to do our jobs simply by putting on a pair of electronic gloves. But I can't help wondering what happens when those robots become capable of performing the same work without us. That's a conversation I think we need to start having now, before this technology becomes commonplace. The $500 million investment shows how much confidence major tech investors have in Genesis AI. The company has ambitious plans to bring Eno into workplaces, and we're getting closer to seeing how robots like these could change the way businesses operate. Genesis says people participating in its training program voluntarily opt in, which is important. But I think there's still a bigger conversation to have about what happens after these robots learn the job. If companies eventually use them to take over certain responsibilities, employees deserve to understand how that could affect their future.

item.title: Millions could lose paid benefits due to Congress ignoring decades of Social Security warnings: experts
item.description: Ron Johnson's report blasts Social Security as a "Ponzi scheme," tracing the program's insolvency to a 1977 law tying benefits to wages, not inflation.
item.content:encoded:
A panel filled with top economists, including a Nobel Peace Prize winner, warned Congress decades ago that their reforms to Social Security could spell disaster. 

Now, experts tell Fox News Digital that group from a bygone era was right, as the safety-net program hurtles toward a crisis that could affect millions. 

"Social Security benefits were put on autopilot back in 1977," Andrew Biggs, a senior fellow of the American Enterprise Institute, told Fox News Digital. "Since then, Congress has done as little as it possibly could."

Senate Budget Committee Chair Ron Johnson, R-Wis., unveiled a report on the decades-old program that blasted it as a "Ponzi scheme," and warned that Social Security’s slide into insolvency began in the 1970s, when, despite warnings, lawmakers opted to tie benefit growth to wages rather than inflation.

AMERICANS MISLED ON SOCIAL SECURITY FOR DECADES AS CLOCK COUNTS DOWN ON BENEFITS, EXPLOSIVE REPORT REVEALS

Johnson wrote in his report that at the time, an expert panel was formed that warned lawmakers that if they were to tie benefits to inflation, "Social Security would likely be sustainable today."

Still, lawmakers at the time ran with their own amendments to the program, which were signed into law by former President Jimmy Carter in December 1977.

"What they said in 1977 was if you index benefit growth to wages, you're effectively building a solvency crisis into the program," Biggs said. "You are over-promising, you're going to build in benefits that the current system can't afford to pay, and you're committing future taxpayers to pay rates of taxes that the taxpayers in 1977 weren't willing to pay."

In the decades since, Congress has done little to change the program.

SENATE REPUBLICANS BREAK THROUGH WASHINGTON GRIDLOCK WITH MASSIVE AMERICAN ENERGY, DATA CENTER OVERHAUL

Romina Boccia, the Cato Institute’s director of budget and entitlement policy, told Fox News Digital that’s largely because lawmakers have not had the political will to do it.

She agreed with Johnson that Social Security was effectively a "Ponzi scheme," and said "there's this misconception that a lot of Americans think that Social Security is a retirement savings program."

"But for that, you would actually need to have savings occur in the system, and there would need to be assets that would be invested in earning returns," Boccia said. "That's not the case. We're talking about a pay-as-you-go program."

One of the side effects of Congress’ lack of action to rein in the program is that the wage growth formula relies on workers in the economy contributing with their paychecks.

Boccia noted that as the decades have gone on, "We've seen a severe decline in the number of workers compared to the number of retirees collecting benefits as a result of a decline in fertility."

DEMOCRATS COULD ENTER CONGRESSIONAL MAJORITY IN A GOVERNMENT SHUTDOWN

Congress’ last real successful effort to reform Social Security came in the early 1980s, Biggs noted, when lawmakers were forced to step in to deal with the "funding crisis" hitting the program.

"They raised taxes. They increased the retirement age. So they did this with months to spare to fix Social Security," Biggs said. "It's not something they wanted to do, but they were forced to do."

"Now in 2032, we're going to face the same situation, where Congress will be forced to take action sometime before the trust fund runs out in 2032, not because they want to, but because they're forced to do it," he continued.

If Social Security’s trust fund runs dry by 2032, Americans’ benefits would be slashed and the onus of paying for the shortfall would add trillions more to the nation’s debt.

But Johnson, in his report, declared that the Social Security problem could not be fixed between now and then because of Congress’ inaction for the last several decades, and he suggested that the solution would be to repeal a possible benefits reduction as the program’s trust fund heads toward insolvency in just under seven years.

Biggs, who was part of former President George W. Bush’s effort to reform Social Security over two decades ago, said that had Congress taken action "25 years ago, you could fix Social Security in barely noticeable ways."

"There is no easy fix to Social Security today, and that stems entirely from the fact that every year, when Congress has had the opportunity to fix Social Security, they chose to duck the issue for political reasons and kick the can down the road," Biggs said.

Boccia disagreed with Johnson’s solution and contended that the real answer was one that lawmakers of yesterday and today would be hesitant to approach — raising taxes.

"The real way to think about this is that there's almost no way to imagine Congress would let those benefit cuts take effect," Boccia said. "It will be so politically toxic. So most likely they're going to try to find a different solution."

"The last time the trust fund was running out of money in 1982, Congress put together a commission and then voted on a bill that increased taxes and reduced benefits, including raising the social security retirement age," she continued. "The problem is that the funding gap now is much larger, more than two times bigger than it was in the ‘80s."

item.title: Visa, Mastercard and JPMorgan customer data leaked
item.description: JPMorgan Chase says hackers accessed marketing data at third-party vendors as an extortion group leaks records tied to Visa and Mastercard customers.
item.content:encoded:
You trust your bank to protect your money. But how much do you know about the outside companies that also handle your personal information? That's a question worth asking after a ransomware group leaked customer data linked to Visa, Mastercard and JPMorgan Chase.

On Nov. 19, 2026, The Wall Street Journal reported that hackers had leaked information allegedly linked to thousands of customers of the three financial companies. The reported exposure involved third-party service providers that work with the financial companies. Now, customers are left wondering what information hackers obtained and whether they need to take action.

Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.

Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.

A SCAMMER HAS YOUR NAME, PHONE NUMBER AND ADDRESS. WHAT CAN THEY ACTUALLY DO?

A cyber extortion group known as n0n claimed to have stolen information associated with the three financial companies. According to Reuters, the group posted claims on Nov. 16 about obtaining cardholder engagement records. These allegedly included extensive marketing activity associated with tens of thousands of email addresses. The group also posted claims involving Visa and Mastercard that same day.

The reported cyberattack involved outside service providers that handle information for financial institutions. Some of the records appear connected to customer marketing activities and cardholder benefit programs. However, several important questions remain unanswered. The companies have not publicly identified all the affected vendors, and investigators have yet to establish whether one compromised provider was responsible for all three reported exposures.

JPMorgan Chase confirmed that third-party service providers were targeted in a cyberattack. In a statement to CyberGuy, a JPMorgan Chase spokesperson said, "Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses."

The bank says its services remain operational. It also plans to contact affected customers where appropriate and offer support, including complimentary credit monitoring. Addressing the transaction processing delays that affected multiple banks earlier this week, the spokesperson added, "There is no connection to service disruption some customers experienced earlier this week."

According to Reuters, leaked records appeared to contain more than 16,000 JPMorgan Chase customer email addresses and 124 bank employee email addresses. Some entries also included phone numbers and postal codes. Reuters could not independently verify the authenticity of the records.

Mastercard also acknowledged an incident involving an outside provider. However, the company says the exposed information was limited to email addresses belonging to a small subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit program. In a statement to CyberGuy, Mastercard said the incident involved non-payment information. "There is no impact to the Mastercard payment network or the ability for people to use their cards," Mastercard said.

The company also confirmed that the exposure has been contained. Its teams are working with the affected provider to support cardholders as needed. Mastercard has not publicly identified the benefit program involved or disclosed an exact number of affected customers. The company also has not indicated that payment-card numbers were exposed.

Visa has responded to CyberGuy about the reported cybersecurity incident involving a third-party service provider in the Asia-Pacific region. The company says its own systems and payment information were unaffected.

In a statement, the company said, "Visa is aware of these claims. They are associated with an incident involving a third-party service provider in Asia Pacific. Visa’s systems were not involved and were not impacted. No payments data such as card numbers were affected. This is unrelated to any of the system disruptions across different industries this past week."

However, Visa has not identified the service provider or disclosed how many customers may have been affected. The company also has not specified what non-payment information, if any, was exposed.

So far, the companies' statements point primarily to customer information held by outside service providers. Mastercard says its payment network remains secure, while Visa says payment-card numbers were unaffected. JPMorgan Chase has identified potentially exposed marketing data. There has been no verified indication that customer banking passwords were stolen or that hackers accessed funds through this incident.

However, stolen contact information can still create problems. Criminals may use names or email addresses to make phishing messages appear more convincing. You could receive an email claiming your bank detected suspicious activity related to the recent cyberattack. The message might direct you to a fake website designed to steal your login information. We've covered how convincing these scams can be in our article about fake bank security alerts that trick customers into sharing personal information.

9 WARNING SIGNS OF IDENTITY THEFT YOU SHOULD NEVER IGNORE

You do not need to assume your account has been compromised. However, there are several practical steps I recommend taking to reduce your exposure to follow-up scams.

Be cautious of unexpected emails or text messages claiming your Visa, Mastercard or JPMorgan Chase account needs immediate attention. Scammers may reference a real cyberattack to make their messages more convincing. They could also claim that your card will be suspended unless you verify your information. Don't click links or open attachments in suspicious messages. Instead, open your bank's official app or type its website address directly into your browser. You can also call the number printed on the back of your card. Using strong antivirus software can provide additional protection by helping detect malicious links and downloads before they cause damage. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at CyberGuy.com

A scammer may call pretending to be from your bank's fraud department. The caller might already know your name or email address and claim that a recent breach put your account at risk. The scammer may then ask you to read back a one-time verification code sent to your phone. That code could allow someone to access your account or approve an unauthorized transaction. Never share a verification code with someone who contacts you unexpectedly. Also, never transfer money to another account because a caller claims it will keep your funds safe. Legitimate bank representatives will not ask you to move your money to a supposedly safe account.

Enable transaction notifications through your bank or credit card app. These alerts can help you spot unfamiliar purchases without waiting for your monthly statement. Check your recent activity and report anything suspicious immediately. Even though the companies have not reported a compromise of their payment networks, monitoring your accounts remains a useful security habit.

Make sure your banking and primary email accounts use unique passwords. If you have reused passwords across accounts, replace them with strong alternatives. A password manager can help you generate and store them securely. Turn on multifactor authentication wherever available. If your bank supports passkeys or security keys, consider using them. An authenticator app is generally a stronger option than SMS codes, although it can still be vulnerable to certain phishing attacks. There is currently no verified evidence that passwords were exposed in this incident. These precautions can help protect your accounts against separate attacks. For more details, see our guide to whether bank text codes are enough to protect you.

JPMorgan Chase says it will contact affected customers where appropriate and offer support, including complimentary credit monitoring. If you receive a breach notification, confirm that it came from your financial institution before clicking an enrollment link or sharing personal information. Credit monitoring can help you identify suspicious changes to your credit reports. However, it cannot stop someone from sending phishing emails or impersonating your bank. You should also be suspicious of anyone demanding payment to activate complimentary protection offered after a breach.

A credit freeze makes it harder for criminals to open new credit accounts in your name. You can place one for free through Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. You must contact each credit bureau separately. A freeze does not affect your credit score, and you can temporarily lift it when you need to apply for credit. If only your name and email address were exposed, a freeze may not be necessary because of this incident alone. However, it can provide broader protection, especially if a breach involves more sensitive identifiers such as a Social Security number.

An exposed email address becomes more useful to scammers when they can connect it with other personal details found online. Consider removing unnecessary information from public profiles and checking what data broker websites have collected about you. A personal data removal service can also help request the removal of information from participating people-search sites. These services cannot erase information already stolen in a cyberattack. However, reducing the amount of personal information publicly available may make it harder for criminals to build convincing profiles for targeted scams. You should also use your phone's spam filtering features and reputable antivirus software to help block suspicious messages or malicious downloads. Get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web: Cyberguy.com

If you clicked a suspicious banking link or shared personal information, take action quickly. What you do next depends on what happened.

You can also report suspected fraud through ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

I've always believed that protecting your financial information requires knowing who has access to it. This latest incident shows how complicated that has become. You can do everything right with your bank account, yet an outside company handling your personal information could still experience a cyberattack. Most of us have little say in which vendors our financial institutions use, and we rarely know how much information those companies collect. I appreciate that Visa, Mastercard and JPMorgan Chase provided statements about the incident. It's reassuring that payment services remain operational, but I'd like to see more transparency about the outside providers involved and exactly what customer information they were holding. Until we have those answers, I would pay close attention to unexpected messages claiming to be from a financial institution. If someone contacts you about a problem with your account, verify it yourself before taking action.

If your bank shares your personal information with outside companies, shouldn't you have a right to know exactly who has it? And would a data leak like this make you reconsider which financial institutions you trust? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com

item.title: MICHAEL RUIZ: Half of California's DAs sue Newsom over death row clemency
item.description: Gavin Newsom faces a lawsuit from 29 district attorneys and victims' families who say his mass clemency for 548 death row inmates skipped victim notice.
item.content:encoded:
District attorneys in half of California's 58 counties have signed onto a lawsuit alongside victims' families and law enforcement groups against term-limited Gov. Gavin Newsom over his lame-duck move to grant clemency to 548 death row inmates in the Golden State.

Many of the prosecutors had publicly condemned the governor's move shortly after he announced it earlier this month.

"Only this Court can stop the Governor’s disregard of the law — his abuse of power," former Sacramento District Attorney Anne Marie Schubert wrote in the 58-page petition, filed Monday. "His eleventh-hour decision to grant commutation en masse intentionally disregarded the statutorily required notice to the victims of these heinous crimes and the prosecutors who obtained those convictions and penalties, and it even interfered with this Court’s mandatory duty to meaningfully review his decisions."

Schubert, who said she worked through the weekend on the filing, is the president and CEO of the Criminal Justice Legal Foundation, which is spearheading the lawsuit on behalf of 29 district attorneys and the families of more than two dozen victims.

MICHAEL RUIZ: CALIFORNIA PROSECUTORS REVOLT AFTER NEWSOM ORDERS STATE'S WORST KILLERS OFF DEATH ROW

Marc Klaas, whose 12-year-old daughter Polly was kidnapped at knifepoint from a slumber party at her mother's house and strangled to death in 1993, is among the petitioners. Polly's killer, Richard Allen Davis, has been on death row since 1996.

Other victims' families include those of slain 8-year-old Gabriel Fernandez, Placer County Sheriff's Detective Mike Davis, Pittsburg Police Officer Larry Lasater, Sacramento Deputy Danny Paul Oliver, and five U.S. Forest Service firefighters killed battling the 40,000-acre Esperanza Fire in 2006 — among others.

Read the filing:

MICHAEL RUIZ: DA IDENTIFIES 49 LOCAL KILLERS SLATE FOR NEWSOM"S DEATH ROW CLEMENCY — AND THEIR CRIMES

"Given what so many of these families have been through for so long, the impact in this case is exceptionally severe, as documented in the declarations filed with this petition," Schubert wrote in the filing. "The Governor’s assurance that the perpetrators will never be released is obviously cruelly false."

The move has even caught the attention of the White House, with President Donald Trump, Attorney General Todd Blanche and FBI Director Kash Patel expected to meet with some of the victims' families Monday.

"Governor Newsom is failing these innocent victims and their families by refusing to carry out justice against these heinous murderers," said Lauren Bis, a White House spokeswoman. "He is playing politics with public safety. President Trump will always stand with innocent victims and will continue to restore law and order and deliver safer communities."

California hasn't carried out an execution in 20 years despite having the largest death row in the country, and Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra is expected to continue the moratorium when he takes office. The death penalty remains on the books as more than a symbolic punishment, however, and condemned inmates are excluded from benefiting from some of the state's criminal justice reforms.

CALIFORNIA SUED OVER POLICY THAT COULD FREE SERIAL KILLERS AS LACI PETERSON'S FRIEND SOUNDS ALARM

BIDEN CLEMENCY BLITZ LEFT DOJ SCRAMBLING AS MANY COMMUTATIONS BYPASSED NORMAL VETTING, EMAILS SHOW

Newsom has argued that the prisoners in question are not eligible for other reforms that could eventually lead to further sentence reductions or even their release. His office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the lawsuit.

But with capital punishment off the table, critics like Orange County District Attorney Todd Spitzer, who announced his own petition Monday, warn that condemned inmates are incrementally moving closer to further leniency.

Newsom wrote in an open letter to California residents that the state "cannot morally kill" the hundreds of people on its death row.

"I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California's values, undermines the foundations of our legal system, and diminishes each of us," he wrote — later acknowledging that those who would benefit from his move "caused indescribable suffering to victims, their families, communities, and our state as a whole."

The Supreme Court of California is expected to review at least 382 of the inmates convicted of multiple felony offenses before Newsom's clemency would be official. According to Schubert's filing, additional inmates who meet the review criteria may not yet have been identified, arguing that Newsom may have relied on incomplete rap sheets when compiling the list.

FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

Still, some experts say the case faces significant hurdles.

"Newsom has broad authority as governor to commute sentences and issue pardons," said Neama Rahmani, a Los Angeles trial attorney and former federal prosecutor. "It may be controversial, but there is little prosecutors and victims can do to prevent it."

California's victims' rights law, which includes the right for victims and their families to be informed of certain clemency and parole decisions ahead of time, may not apply to the commutations, he said.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

"There was no application here," Rahmani told Fox News Digital.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB

Schubert appeared to anticipate this line of reasoning in her filing.

"If the statutory sunshine process can be defeated merely by the absence of a formal application, the worst abuses would be unregulated, while inmates following the normal procedures would have their applications regulated," she wrote. "That would be backwards and an absurd result."

GOT A TIP?

Thousands of jurors and hundreds of judges have been involved in the convictions and death sentences of the inmates set to benefit from Newsom's clemency, she wrote. Many of them "set aside their personal views" in the process.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

"Governor Newsom decided his personal views should override all those who actually participated in the process, followed and applied the law," she wrote. "He did none of that, as he freely admits. That alone is an abuse of power that must not stand."

GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL

According to the Death Penalty Information Center, which tracks capital punishment across the United States, Newsom had not granted a clemency request to any death row inmate before this month's announcement, despite a longstanding opposition to capital punishment.

In fact, no California governor had commuted a death sentence since Ronald Reagan spared a man with previously undiagnosed brain damage in 1967.

Fox News Digital reached out to Newsom's office for comment.

item.title: Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson fights to stay on 2027 ballot amid City Hall exodus, credit warning
item.description: A budget dispute, a third CFO departure in roughly a year and a credit warning are adding pressure as Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson prepares to defend his record with voters.
item.content:encoded:
Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson (D) is fighting to keep his name on the 2027 ballot at the exact moment his administration is engulfed in a fiscal and leadership meltdown at City Hall.

Election officials are reviewing challenges to more than 25,000 of Johnson's nominating signatures ahead of the Feb. 23, 2027, mayoral election — a threshold fight unfolding just days after his third chief financial officer in 10 months abruptly resigned, Standard & Poor's placed Chicago's credit rating on negative watch and the City Council voted 45-5 to investigate three years of city financial reporting for possible misstatements.

Despite the mounting pressure, Johnson brushed off questions about whether he will survive the ballot challenge.

"Yeah, feeling just fine, I'm going to be on the ballot," Johnson told ABC 7 Chicago about the challenge. "Looking forward to building the safest, most affordable big city in America, and we're going to continue to do that work."

CHICAGO'S 12-LANGUAGE BALLOTS MAKE ELECTIONS 'HARDER TO MONITOR,' ILLINOIS GOP CHAIR WARNS

Johnson needs 12,500 valid signatures to qualify for Chicago's Feb. 23, 2027, mayoral ballot. Hearing officers at the Chicago Board of Elections are reviewing more than 25,000 signatures challenged by supporters of perennial mayoral candidate Willie Wilson. Johnson's campaign says 6,718 signatures were not challenged and projects that he would finish with 14,788 valid signatures if the first day's 32% validation rate holds. That would put him 2,288 signatures above the requirement, but the figure is the campaign's estimate, not a final board tally. The objectors say early rulings are favoring their challenge, and the review remains unresolved.

The turmoil inside City Hall accelerated following the sudden departure of chief financial officer Ashlee Gabrysch, who said continuing in the role would "compromise my integrity and professional obligations." Johnson later said she "wasn't the right fit."

"It’s yet another high-level change in the mayor’s administration, and is a sign of continuing turmoil and a lack of direction at a very key time for the city, especially for him heading into a mayoral election," David Greising, CEO of the Better Government Association, told CBS Chicago following Gabrysch's abrupt exit.

A survey of 1,108 adults by NORC at the University of Chicago, conducted Sept. 13-23, found that 22.2% approved of Johnson's job performance, while 52.9% disapproved and 24.8% had no opinion. The survey predates both the current petition review and Gabrysch's departure.

4 OF NATION'S LARGEST CITIES NOW LED BY SOCIALIST MAYORS AFTER TUESDAY'S ELECTION, AFFECTING TENS OF MILLIONS

Meanwhile, Johnson's proposed $17.6 billion 2027 budget is intended to close an $882.4 million gap, but a 28-member City Council bloc told him it did not see the votes needed to pass his tax proposals.

Standard & Poor's ultimately placed Chicago's BBB general-obligation rating on negative CreditWatch, citing the budget stalemate and management instability. The agency said there was at least a 50% chance of a downgrade within 90 days, which could raise the city's borrowing costs.

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

The City Council eventually voted 45-5 on Wednesday to authorize an independent review of three years of financial reporting for possible material or intentional misstatements.

Fox News Digital reached out to Mayor Brandon Johnson's office and campaign, the Chicago Board of Elections, and Christopher Berry, a University of Chicago professor and faculty director of the Mansueto Institute for Urban Innovation, which commissioned the ChicagoSpeaks survey conducted by NORC. They did not respond by publication.

item.title: Meghan Markle’s brand gets Oprah push, but expert says duchess still has ‘a credibility problem’
item.description: Oprah Winfrey's "Favorite Things" list features Meghan Markle's As Ever gift basket, but experts say the duchess still faces a "credibility problem."
item.content:encoded:
Meghan Markle may have Oprah Winfrey's stamp of approval, but experts say even the queen of daytime television can't guarantee the Duchess of Sussex something money can't buy: credibility.

Winfrey's "Favorite Things" list for 2026 debuted Nov. 12, and Meghan's As Ever The Signature Basket landed a spot.

But while Winfrey's endorsement could help Meghan sell her products, experts say winning over the public may prove a much tougher challenge.

MEGHAN MARKLE'S FAILED MARTHA STEWART DREAMS MOCKED BY COMEDIAN: 'SHE WAS SLINGING JAM'

"Meghan doesn't have a name recognition problem," royal expert Kinsey Schofield told Fox News Digital. "She has a credibility problem, in my opinion."

"Oprah has spent decades convincing Americans that her recommendations are worth their money. Meghan is benefiting from that trust," the host of YouTube’s "Kinsey Schofield Unfiltered" said. "But I also think Oprah's association with the Sussexes has come at a reputational cost. Her 2021 interview attracted criticism for its lack of challenging follow-up questions. Oprah's endorsement may generate sales, but I don't think either woman automatically improves the other's credibility anymore."

Meghan launched As Ever in 2025 as a rebranding of her earlier concept, American Riviera Orchard, marking the Duchess of Sussex's return to the lifestyle space she once occupied with her pre-royal blog, "The Tig." The brand debuted with a tight, curated collection of small-batch essentials — including raspberry spreads, wildflower honey with honeycomb, crêpe and shortbread cookie mixes, flower sprinkles, and herbal teas — which famously sold out within an hour of going live.

PRINCE HARRY, MEGHAN MARKLE FEEDING THE 'PUBLICITY MACHINE' DESPITE PRIVACY DEMANDS: EXPERT

Winfrey's addition of Meghan's gift basket on her Favorite Things list will drive brand awareness and sales heading into the holiday season, according to British royal expert Hilary Fordwich.

"This celebrity lifestyle brand arena is such a frightfully crowded space, so such a high-profile celebrity endorsement certainly is a welcome differentiator," she added. "Yet Oprah does feature many products, including from other famous friends."

The business venture remains the centerpiece of Meghan's post-royal business strategy, blending her California aesthetic with direct-to-consumer retail.

Meghan's brand wouldn't have the same star power, however, without Winfrey's push, brand expert Doug Eldridge told Fox News Digital.

"Would Markle have the mic if she never married Prince Harry? No. She was the fourth lead on a short-lived legal drama on the USA Network," the founder of Achilles PR explained. Would As Ever be conversationally relevant were it not created by an erstwhile Duchess and promoted by the Queen of American TV? No."

"Objectively speaking, it’s an overpriced line of basic household goods hitting the U.S. market at a time of inflation, spiking gas prices, and overall economic uncertainty," Eldridge added. "That said, seemingly every celebrity these days has their own brand of tequila, wine, or hard seltzer brand. The shelf life for celebrity influence is fleeting, so most of these personalities are branching out (and cashing in) while they still can."

However, Winfrey endorsing Meghan's product for a second time is "highly significant," according to one royal expert.

"It shows that Oprah is still behind Meghan and that counts in Hollywood," royal commentator Richard Fitzwilliams told Fox News Digital. "As its sales and profits are undisclosed, we cannot know how successful it actually is. Because it is linked to Meghan, it has been the subject of enormous speculation, but we don’t know turnover, costs and profit, if any."

While critics question whether Winfrey's endorsement can boost Meghan's credibility or ensure As Ever's long-term success, others say the media mogul's continued support proves the duchess still has powerful allies and influence in Hollywood.

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

"Meghan's enduring relationship with Oprah shows that the Hollywood outcast narrative really doesn't hold any water," royal commentator Meredith Constant explained to Fox News Digital. "At the end of the day, business is business," she added. "Plus, we know Oprah actually likes As Ever's products; she's been quoted in the past as saying that she got to enjoy Meghan's recipes before they became a part of the As Ever brand."
