item.title: Mamdani’s plan to dismantle NYPD’s riot unit ripped as ‘smoke and mirrors’ by former force leaders
item.description: Ex-NYPD chief John Chell calls Mayor Zohran Mamdani's plan to gut the Strategic Response Group "smoke and mirrors," claiming the unit will be rebranded.
item.content:encoded:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's plan to gut the city’s tactical police unit is not what is seems, two former high-ranking NYPD officials tell Fox News Digital.

They argue the stunt is a political sleight of hand in which specialized officers responsible for handling violent protests will be rebranded under a different name despite the socialist mayor's promise to disband it completely.

"The problem is…day-to-day New Yorkers don't understand all this gas lighting," former NYPD Chief John Chell told Fox News Digital. "And they feel the angst of it."

"But at the end of all that, this is nothing more than smoke and mirrors," he added.

EXCLUSIVE: RETIRED POLICE SERGEANT ISSUES WARNING OVER MAMDANI'S NYPD SHAKE-UP AHEAD OF THANKSGIVING PARADE

The move to dissolve the Strategic Response Group (SRG) and replace it with a "first-of-its-kind" civilian dialogue team fulfills one of Mamdani's campaign promises — noted in the first sentence of his news release on the move.

But Chell and retired NYPD inspector Paul Mauro are questioning whether it's all a facade to please the mayor's left-wing base and is a restructuring rather than a disbandment. They say the unit will likely be rebuilt under a new name to continue dealing with mass protests, major crimes and counterterrorism.

"The con here is that the SRG is simply being rebranded into an unknown name right now," Chell said.

"First of all, Mamdani did add…that there will be uniformed police standing by to take more forceful enforcement if necessary," Mauro said. "So what really changed? Well, he changed the name of that unit and he inserted this civilian unit between those uniformed cops and the protesters."

The newly proposed civilian-led Community Dialogue and De-escalation Division (CDDD) is meant to work as a buffer between protesters and the on-duty police that will remain present at large demonstrations.

"Socialism and public safety do not go hand in hand," Chell insisted.

Mamdani’s office did not respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment on the criticism of his plan.

NY COP CALLS FOR POLICE PROTECTIONS AFTER PROTESTER HE ARRESTED SHOWED UP TO HIS HOUSE, HARASSED HIS FAMILY

Both former NYPD officials warned that relying on civilians to mediate rowdy crowds could delay police intervention if a peaceful protest turns into a violent riot. This, he said, could leave officers responding to an escalating situation rather than preventing it in the first place.

"Once a cop, wherever they're assigned, becomes reactive versus proactive — public safety suffers," Chell said. "And [when cops] become reactive, they tend to hold back and that can get them hurt, and it can get civilians hurt."

"That is one of the risks inherent in this thing," Mauro added. "That you deploy the civilians, they're trying to talk…and by the time the civilians turn around and say, ‘Police, we need help,’ it may be too late."

SRG receives information from NYPD’s Intelligence and Counterterrorism Bureau to be kept aware of known or potentially dangerous demonstrations that will require specialized training to deescalate.

The SRG unit is trained to handle crowds that have turned violent, beginning with verbal de-escalation. The physical training teaches officers how to get a noncomplying individual and into police vans. A common tactic used by the SRG is bicycle crowd management where officers can line up their bikes to build a barricade in crowds, using those formations for crowd control.

"The purpose of the SRG was to make sure that you had highly trained officers who could diffuse, spin down, but then control if need be, protests that were getting out of hand," Mauro said. "That's why they were only deployed in about 6% of the instances."

MAMDANI CLASHES WITH DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS' PUSH TO ABOLISH POLICE AND PRISONS

In a budget hearing earlier this year it was noted the SRG did not often deal with peaceful protests, and were mostly only deployed for protests that turned violent. In 2025, NYPD reportedly facilitated 4,255 protests and the SRG was available for roughly 6% of them.

Critics of the SRG, including the ACLU's New York affiliate, say the unit is inherently violent due to its counterterrorism specialization that they claim "suppress protesters" and disregards "focus on First Amendment protections."

The training manual, reviewed by Fox News Digital, distinguishes between "peaceful/compliant" crowds and those deemed "violent/non-compliant." It also identifies three categories of protesters: "everyday citizen," "professional" and "anarchist."

The first identifier under the "everyday citizen" protester immediately acknowledges that they are honoring their First Amendment right to organize.

FLORIDA EYES POACHING NYPD OFFICERS AFTER MAMDANI DISMANTLES ELITE UNIT

Despite the dismantling of the SRG, Mamdani's plan would still likely require police officers be present at larger demonstrations. The new civilian-led group, however, would be there to attempt to de-escalate the protesters if it should show signs of turning violent.

Mamdani has not yet said when the civilian-led team will be established or take the streets. He also announced the creation of the First Amendment Support Team (FAST), a 30-officer NYPD unit, that will help deescalate crowds while the CDDD is being developed.

Chell, who has announced he will be running for mayor of New York City in 2029 when Mamdani would likely be seeking a second term, said he doubts the new team will take form until at least 2028 – if ever.

"What's scary about all this, the mentality of how the mayor and his staff and his socialist friends want to run this city," Chell said.

"If they get everything they want, we're gonna be a third world city and I don't know if we can ever get it back."

item.title: Ukraine deals major blow to Putin’s Crimea lifeline, European intel assessment claims
item.description: Gen. Philip Breedlove says cutting the Kerch Bridge will severely damage Russia's ability to resupply Crimea as Kyiv lands three strikes in four days.
item.content:encoded:
Ukraine's repeated attacks on the Kerch Bridge, one of Russian President Vladimir Putin's most prized infrastructure projects, have dealt a potentially significant blow to Moscow's military supply routes into occupied Crimea, raising questions about Russia's ability to sustain operations as both sides prepare for a difficult winter.

A European intelligence assessment dated Nov. 18 and obtained by Fox News Digital describes Ukraine's latest assault as likely its most successful attack on the heavily defended crossing, following a coordinated campaign targeting Russian air defenses, radar and electronic warfare systems.

Ret. Gen. Philip Breedlove, former NATO Supreme Allied Commander Europe, told Fox News Digital the consequences could extend far beyond the destruction of a symbolic Russian landmark. "The Russians are extremely limited in how they get supplies to Crimea and cutting the Kerch bridge will severely, severely damage their ability to resupply Crimea," Breedlove said.

UKRAINE HITS PUTIN'S PRIZED BRIDGE IN RECORD DRONE BLITZ AS KREMLIN TELLS LAWMAKERS TO PREPARE FOR 'VICTORY'

On Nov. 17, Ukrainian missiles and drones struck the 12-mile bridge linking Russia's Krasnodar region to Crimea, collapsing a major section of the roadway into the Kerch Strait and damaging the adjacent railway.

The crossing, inaugurated by Putin in 2018, has served as both a critical transportation link and a symbol of Russia's annexation of Crimea in 2014.

According to the European intelligence assessment, the attack followed a multiweek Ukrainian operation against Russian defensive systems, intended to weaken the bridge's protection before the main strike.

Ukraine subsequently struck the railway again on Nov.19, temporarily halting train traffic and bringing the number of attacks to three in four days.

The damage has disrupted one of Russia's most direct supply connections to Crimea, which Moscow uses to support military operations in southern Ukraine.

PUTIN LAUNCHES UKRAINE BARRAGE HOURS AFTER TRUMP MEETING AMID ALLEGED RUSSIAN MISSILE BREACH OF NATO AIRSPACE

Russia has developed an alternative land corridor through occupied southern Ukraine, but the European intelligence assessment warns that shifting additional military supplies onto those roads could create significant vulnerabilities.

The assessment identifies slower transportation routes, exposure to Ukrainian drone attacks and pressure on other logistical infrastructure as potential consequences.

Breedlove said Ukraine's campaign should be viewed as an attempt to weaken Russia's hold on the peninsula, rather than simply destroy a bridge. He argued that Russia's options are further constrained by Ukraine's success in challenging Russian naval power in the northern Black Sea.

He pointed out that Ukraine has used maritime and aerial drones to push back Russia's Black Sea Fleet despite lacking large conventional warships.

The European assessment also warns that repairing the bridge could take months. Although limited road traffic might resume within weeks, replacing the collapsed section could take considerably longer, particularly if Ukrainian attacks continue.

Damage above the Kerch–Yenikale Canal could also disrupt shipping between the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov.

UKRAINE'S ATTACKS ON RUSSIA ARE PUSHING PUTIN CLOSER TO NEGOTIATING TABLE, TRUMP NATO AMBASSADOR SAYS

Despite Ukraine's success in striking the bridge, a European intelligence source familiar with Russian strategic assessments offered a pessimistic view of the broader conflict.

"It has more symbolic meaning, but also logistics is paralyzed right now," the source told Fox News Digital, describing the immediate impact of the attacks.

However, the source warned that Moscow is preparing to intensify its winter offensive while using negotiations with Washington to increase political pressure on Kyiv.

"The general trend is not good for Ukraine," the source said.

According to the source, Russia believes it can sustain military pressure long enough to force Ukraine into territorial concessions, particularly in the east.

"They are very convinced that by spring Ukrainians will give up," the source said, describing Moscow's expectations.

Breedlove strongly disputed the assessment that Russia was gaining the upper hand militarily.

"Militarily, the tide is turning against Russia," Breedlove told Fox News Digital, arguing that Russian forces have suffered staggering casualties while making limited battlefield gains.

He said Russian losses in recent months had been extraordinarily high and argued that Moscow's military was failing to achieve significant territorial advances.

Breedlove did, however, acknowledge a distinction between military momentum and the political pressure facing Ukraine.

He suggested that changes in Washington's approach to negotiations could strengthen Putin's position even if Russian forces were struggling on the battlefield.

The competing assessments highlight a central question facing Ukraine: whether its military successes can translate into greater diplomatic leverage before Russia's winter offensive intensifies.

UKRAINE STRIKES 'ONE OF THE LARGEST OIL REFINERIES' IN SOUTHERN RUSSIA AHEAD OF PUTIN-TRUMP MEETING IN CHINA

Putin has threatened retaliation over the bridge attacks, and on Friday Russia launched a massive missile and drone assault against Ukrainian cities, killing at least eight people, according to Ukrainian authorities.

The strikes came hours after Putin appeared alongside President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping at a summit in China, as Washington continued efforts to advance peace negotiations.

The European intelligence assessment warns that further Ukrainian attacks on the Kerch Bridge during repairs are highly likely, potentially prolonging disruptions to Russian supplies.

For Moscow, restoring the crossing is now both a logistical challenge and a political priority. For Kyiv, keeping it vulnerable offers a way to increase the cost of Russia's occupation while demonstrating that even Putin's most heavily defended infrastructure remains within reach.

item.title: DR MARC SIEGEL: Cruise ships can be petri dishes for viruses. Calm may be the best cure
item.description: The CDC reports 148 aboard Princess Cruises' Caribbean Princess fell ill with stomach illness, as norovirus causes over 90% of cruise ship outbreaks.
item.content:encoded:
Fear is more contagious than any pathogen, especially on a cruise ship with a captive audience and a mysterious outbreak.

As reported this week by Fox News Digital, "A Caribbean cruise has taken an uncomfortable turn for nearly 150 passengers and crew members who have fallen sick with stomach illness symptoms — with an infectious disease expert providing important insight into a very ‘common’ issue. A total of 148 people aboard Princess Cruises' Caribbean Princess — 134 passengers and 14 crew members — have reported the symptoms, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)."

The Caribbean Princess ship itself has since been replaced (2004), upgraded, and renovated (2019), but one thing remains unchanged: the propensity for infectious outbreaks aboard cruise ships, as well as the associated worry. Part of the problem on a cruise ship is the small, crowded quarters, the shared spaces, and the fact that seemingly no amount of disinfection is enough. Another problem is the delay in determining the actual pathogen, as is the case currently on the Caribbean Princess, where 148 people have now fallen sick with an unknown stomach illness.

Even if there is nothing that can be done about it other than separation and increased disinfection, as is currently occurring on this ship, simply being able to put a name to the virus helps to calm fears. Cheap, rapid testing aided by artificial intelligence is in the future.

Current rapid PCR testing on a ship the size of the Caribbean Princess takes dozens of expensive machines and many days to complete. It isn’t feasible. Norovirus causes over 90% of these outbreaks—about 10 to 20 per year, including one on this ship earlier this spring.

The company has put out a statement about the cruise saying, "Princess Cruises can confirm that a limited number of guests aboard Caribbean Princess have reported mild gastrointestinal illness. Our crew responded promptly by implementing enhanced sanitation protocols across the ship, including comprehensive cleaning and disinfection measures. While most guests remain unaffected, we are continuing to closely monitor the situation."

But sometimes a mysterious outbreak is due to something far worse than norovirus, where the delay in identification can cost lives. The MV Hondius embarked from Ushuaia, Argentina, on April 1, setting sail on a repositioning cruise offering a specialized ecotourism and research voyage. It was also unknowingly carrying the Andes strain of hantavirus, along with over 150 passengers and 57 crew.

COULD HANTAVIRUS SPREAD ON A CRUISE SHIP? EXPERTS WEIGH RISKS AFTER DEADLY OUTBREAK

This strain can spread human-to-human and can easily be deadly, especially when a person develops hantavirus pulmonary syndrome. One patient, Leo Schilperoord, developed a fever and flu-like symptoms on April 5, yet continued to mingle with passengers until April 10, when he died. A British birdwatcher became ill, and then, on April 22, Mirjam Schilperoord-Huisman developed symptoms. They were taken off the ship at the end of April and brought to Johannesburg, South Africa, for diagnosis and treatment.

Finally, on May 1, 2026, when the ship’s doctor became ill, retired Oregon oncologist and dedicated birdwatcher Dr. Stephen Kornfeld took over.

DR MARC SIEGEL, JENNIFER JOHNSON: MEET THE ANGEL DOCTORS FIGHTING HANTAVIRUS

When I first interviewed Dr. Kornfeld for my new book, "The Angels Among Us," I was amazed to consider the ease with which he transitioned from a birdwatching role to putting his life on the line. But then I realized that it was simply a return to the same manner he’d developed for decades as a highly regarded and beloved oncologist in Oregon who calmed fears in the face of a patient’s uncertain future.

As he said to me, the small group on that ship, which had by then traveled together for weeks and gone on many excursions, was like a family. "I know the limitations of equipment and medications on the ship. I know that if things become life-threatening for the sick people, my ability to intervene will be somewhat limited. At the same time, I know that I can just be reassuring to everyone on the boat, the crew, and the passengers. Letting them know that there is still a medical presence, that if other people get sick, there will at least be somebody to talk with them and try to help them. And I ultimately think this provides more of a service to the people on board than my actual care."

DR MARC SIEGEL: HANTAVIRUS CRUISE OUTBREAK IS ALARMING, BUT FEAR IS SPREADING FASTER THAN FACTS

Out there on the high seas, Kornfeld became an instrument of divine mercy, radiating a deep, spiritual strength that kept the frightened passengers from falling into total despair. By spreading calm, he slowed the spread of the virus, as people were far more capable of complying with restrictions and isolation.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Finally, on May 4, it was determined in South Africa, where two patients were taken (Mirjam Schilperoord-Huisman ended up dying there), that this was the Andes strain of the hantavirus. Lengthy quarantines followed passengers disembarking in mid-May, and I visited the National Quarantine Center at the University of Nebraska Medical Center, where several patients were held in the same place I had once visited at the onset of the COVID pandemic.

Overall, there were 13 reported cases and three deaths. Weeks later, it was finally confirmed that there was no spread beyond the 13 cases on the ship.

Travel on cruise ships can be relaxing and rejuvenating, especially if you are traveling to archipelagos otherwise unreachable. But when you are suddenly closed in with a threatening virus, whether it is a mild stomach bug or a deadly pulmonary virus, a ship can become a traveling petri dish—until an angel of healing like Stephen Kornfeld is sent by God to provide succor and thereby limit the spread.

item.title: 2028 presidential contender under fire from state auditor over waste, fraud, abuse fears: 'Troubling response'
item.description: Kentucky's top auditor says $1.5 billion in taxpayer waste was uncovered, accusing Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear of brushing off Medicaid and SNAP findings.
item.content:encoded:
Kentucky’s top auditor says her office has uncovered $1.5 billion in taxpayer waste across state government and accused Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear, widely believed to have presidential aspirations, of brushing off the findings instead of helping fix them.

"I wish I could say that I had more support and help from the governor's office in Kentucky, but I haven't really and that's one of the reasons why I'm very public with our reports. I'm very public with our findings, because I need the public's help," Ball said in an interview this week at a State Financial Officers Foundation (SFOF) conference in Philadelphia.

"I need the backlash that comes when you see money just being flushed down the toilet, when you see that you're losing money, especially in Medicaid. It's money that should go to people who are actually in need, and we're losing those dollars."

Over the past year, Ball’s office flagged $836 million in wasteful Medicaid spending that was primarily driven by multi-state concurrent enrollment, where Kentucky continued paying monthly managed care capitation fees for individuals simultaneously enrolled in Medicaid in up to eight other states.

TRUMP ADMIN PAUSING OVER $1B IN MEDICAID PAYMENTS TO MINNESOTA, CALIFORNIA OVER FRAUD, COMPLIANCE CONCERNS

Her audits also flagged ineligible noncitizens receiving benefits, single Social Security numbers being used by up to 10 people at once, duplicate individual payments, and roughly $100 million in SNAP benefit errors, bringing the total waste she cited across state benefit programs to $1.5 billion.

"I have had conversations with the governor's staff," Ball explained. "We are always letting the governor know, 'Hey, this is what we found.' We also offer solutions all the time. And typically what I get back is, like for the $836 million of Medicaid dollars that we found, is that, 'Well, that happens everywhere. You know, that's not unique to us.' And that's really a troubling response. If your attitude is like, 'Well, it's not just us, you know, we're not really doing a horrible job because it happens other places too,' that explains why problems like this continue."

RNC RIPS BESHEAR'S 'WOKE TRANS RECORD' OVER VETO OF KENTUCKY GIRLS' SPORTS BILL

Additionally, Ball’s office released a report earlier this year outlining spending by Beshear’s executive branch in fiscal year 2025 that, while not illegal, flagged what she called "massive" issues of extravagant spending of tax dollars that "needs to stop."

The "concerning expenditures" listed include $183,576 in out-of-state travel costs, including $7,632 for a limousine in Germany; a $17,013 dinner at a Kentucky distillery; and $360,000 for 75 people to attend a two-day conference within the Commonwealth.

"I think one thing that I have realized is that the governor doesn't like bad news. And unfortunately, a lot of times when I come in, and I do an audit, the news that I have is bad," Ball said. "But what I also try to remind people, it's good too, in the sense that I also have a recommendation for how to fix it. So, while it is important to identify the problems — and I do that — I'm also hyper-focused on the solution. And I would encourage the governor to jump in and help me be part of the solution to this. That's not been the experience that I've had. I've not had cooperation, and I would love to have that. I think that that's what Kentuckians deserve."

Beshear’s office has repeatedly pushed back on Ball’s criticisms, dismissing her $836 million Medicaid waste estimate as "a wild extrapolation from a small subset" and maintaining that once Kentucky gained access to updated federal cross-check databases, actual multi-state overlap numbers were "nothing remotely close to that."

In a statement to Fox News Digital, his office said the governor has "created a fiscally responsible administration, securing six consecutive budget surpluses, the five best years on record for economic investment and upgrades from all three major bond rating agencies while also cutting income and property taxes. His management of the state is delivering positive results, so hardworking Kentuckians can live better lives."

Beshear's office added that Ball's report has "significant errors and inaccuracies" and suggested she focus on "real threats looming in Kentucky due to Trump's ‘Big, Ugly Bill,’ which risks the closure of 35 rural hospitals, the jobs of 20,000 healthcare workers and health coverage for thousands of Kentuckians."

When it comes to potential Medicaid waste, fraud and abuse, Ball told Fox News Digital it is unlikely that money can be clawed back, heightening the importance of stopping it before it begins.

The Trump administration has made cracking down on fraud this year and set up the Task Force to Eliminate Fraud in March which has reported that federal agencies have identified $260.7 billion in estimated fraud since January 2025.

Ball told Fox News Digital that heading into 2027, she sees a "tremendous opportunity" to address waste, fraud, and abuse in Kentucky because the "public cares right now, I think, at a level that they've not cared before."

"I've always cared about protecting taxpayer dollars, I've also cared about stopping waste, fraud, and abuse. I care about complying with the law," Ball said. "I think this is this beautiful moment right now where the public deeply cares about it too. So I think I have an opportunity. I think other auditors around the country, other people who are in similar roles, have opportunities like it's never been before where we really can take the effort to stop these things from happening."6408662620112

item.title: Lawmakers warn Americans of vulnerable systems amid streak of outages: 'Something is going on'
item.description: Lawmakers warn America's power grids, water systems and banks are soft targets after a 10-day wave of tech outages raised cybersecurity concerns.
item.content:encoded:
Lawmakers are sounding the alarm over security threats in America's critical infrastructure following a 10-day wave of tech outages across major industries, warning about cybersecurity and the resilience of the nation's increasingly interconnected, vulnerable systems.

"I will tell you from my dealing back in the intelligence world in the Pentagon, this is not normal," Rep. Keith Self, R-Texas, said. "Ask the questions."

"Cybersecurity is a serious issue, and threats are becoming more serious," Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., said.

TIMELINE: AMERICA HITS A TECH WALL AS OUTAGES CRIPPLE EMAIL, GROUND FLIGHTS AND DISRUPT MAJOR BANKS

"These systems are complex," Rep. Pete Ricketts, R-Neb., said. "I used to run a company that had technology. It's not unusual."

The lawmakers' concerns come as the nation continues to experience tech outages, including at the National Security Agency, and grapples with whether the recent disruptions were isolated technical failures or signs of a broader cybersecurity threat.

President Donald Trump's administration says the incidents were unrelated and were not caused by malicious actors. But speculation continues to increase, particularly after Trump fired National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross on Thursday over concerns that he lacked the proper credentials in cybersecurity for the job.

"The question has got to be asked, ‘Is there an offensive cyberattack going on that we're not going to hear about?’" Self said. "Because I don't believe any of the public statements that are made, because something is going on behind the scenes."

RECENT SERVICE OUTAGES NOT STATE-SPONSORED ATTACKS, DNI JAY CLAYTON TESTIFIES

Officials say that as artificial intelligence gets better at spotting holes in a system's security, those systems are coming under more strain as companies try to patch those holes.

Regardless of what caused the disruptions, lawmakers warned that the incidents underscore a broader concern: America's reliance on interconnected technology has created potential vulnerabilities across critical infrastructure, from local water systems and power grids to banking and aviation.

"The localized municipal-based infrastructure in America is a soft target," Sen. Tim Sheehy, R-Mont., told Fox News Digital. "And that's been flagged for decades. We haven't addressed it fully. And I think over the past week, we've seen it's time we get serious about it."

$1M-A-DAY CHINA TECH CRACKDOWN PROPOSED AMID CASCADE OF US CYBER DISRUPTIONS

"Everything's interconnected now, so we've got to be working on security all the time," Sen. John Hoeven, R-N.D., said. "Cybersecurity is a big deal, and it's not just in government, but in business as well, and that's what we're seeing. There's been a number of these incidents around the country now and, obviously, people are concerned about it and we should be."

Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., encouraged keeping conversation around cyber threats and developing U.S. systems to reduce vulnerability as a bipartisan issue.

"If they're interconnected or random, no one really knows because they're putting out a lot of misinformation," Fetterman said. "So we really need to strip out the politics and find out really what it is."

item.title: Nick Saban names three teams above Alabama as college football's true national championship contenders
item.description: Nick Saban says Georgia, Utah and Notre Dame have "the right stuff" in 2026, leaving his former Alabama Crimson Tide off his elite list of three teams.
item.content:encoded:
Nick Saban isn't playing favorites. The former Alabama football head coach said he is not convinced this year’s team has what it takes to make a deep run in this year's College Football Playoff.

During an appearance on "The Pat McAfee Show," Saban identified the teams he believes belong in a tier above the rest of the national championship hopefuls. The seven-time national championship-winning coach pointed to Georgia, Utah and Notre Dame as the teams he views as true contenders.

Alabama was notably not included in that group.

"Me personally, I think there's three teams that have the right stuff," Saban said. "This is no disrespect to Alabama because I think there's probably seven or eight teams that could win the championship, Alabama being one of them, but if you're a betting man and you say, who can run the ball, who can play good defense, and who has a good quarterback?"

Saban acknowledged that teams outside his top three could still make a run, but he believes each has a potential weakness to overcome.

"You would say Georgia has that, Utah has that. Notre Dame has that. Everybody else maybe has a flaw somewhere along the way. They might be able to overcome it, but I think those three teams have the right stuff."

ESPN DISMISSES UTAH UTES AS NATIONAL CHAMPIONSHIP CONTENDERS DESPITE BIG WIN OVER BYU: 'THEY WON'T WIN'

Alabama has built a respectable resume this season. The Crimson Tide have knocked off two ranked teams, Kentucky and South Carolina. They also took Georgia down to the wire in a close loss at home. Since dropping games to the Bulldogs and the Tennessee Volunteers, Alabama has put together a three-game winning streak against SEC opponents.

After the College Football Playoff selection committee released its third rankings earlier this week, chair Hunter Yurachek pointed to Alabama’s overall profile, including its margin of victory.

"I think it's a collection of things for Alabama," Yurachek said. "Not only the margin of wins, their SEC wins, which is close to 23 points a game, but their relative scoring defense is in the top 20, relative scoring offense is in the top five, record strength is in the top 5. Quite honestly, when we watch them on film, when we watch their games, we really feel like they're one of the best three or four teams in the country."'

While Saban offered his assessment Friday, Kalen DeBoer struck a more optimistic tone about Alabama in his third season leading the program.

"I feel like we're more complete as a football team and able to play anybody, anytime, anywhere," DeBoer said. "But you got to go do it."

item.title: LSU women's basketball star MiLaysia Fulwiley faces only misdemeanor charges after arrest
item.description: LSU's MiLaysia Fulwiley faces only misdemeanor fleeing and resisting charges after her arrest, with felony counts dropped and a diversion program planned.
item.content:encoded:
LSU women’s basketball player MiLaysia Fulwiley will face misdemeanor traffic citations stemming from a recent traffic incident.

The felony charges included in her initial booking will now be pursued as misdemeanor counts, the East Baton Rouge District Attorney's Office confirmed Friday. Authorities allege Fulwiley attempted to evade officers during a traffic stop.

District Attorney Hillar Moore said fleeing and resisting an officer would be weighed as misdemeanors. Fulwiley will also be referred to a diversion program to resolve the charges. The initial charges listed at the time of Fulwiley’s booking included aggravated battery and assault, based on allegations that she drove her vehicle into an officer’s vehicle. Fulwiley has denied the police's account.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

State police captain Russell Graham said Friday that his agency reviewed evidence with Moore and agreed with his decision. "After a thorough review with all involved parties, the charges were amended based on the circumstances and evidence presented," State Police said in a written statement provided by Graham.

Fulwiley has not appeared in a game for LSU since her arrest. It remains unclear whether she will return to the team.

ALABAMA DISMISSES DEFENSIVE BACK DRE KIRKPATRICK JR FROM TEAM AFTER BEING ARRESTED FOR SECOND TIME

Fulwiley apologized to police and her teammates.

"Saturday night ended in a situation that never should have happened," she said in a statement released by LSU. "I owe an apology to the officers involved and everyone who calls themselves a Tiger. I also want to apologize to my family and all those who love and support me."

The traffic stop happened near Tiger Stadium in Baton Rouge as the a football game between LSU and Texas was ending.

"Rules and laws apply to everyone, including the instructions of officers working a game night in Baton Rouge," Fulwiley said. "I respect the job those officers do, and I’ll let the legal process run its course. My focus is doing what this program asks of me and earning back the trust of the people who count on me."

Fulwiley scored a season-high 23 points on Nov. 13 during LSU’s 101-37 win over the University of Denver.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: Alabama woman pleads guilty after reportedly using smart glasses to target drug trial witnesses
item.description: Tierra Shatalia Douglas pleaded guilty to conspiracy to retaliate against a witness after targeting people who testified in a federal drug trial.
item.content:encoded:
An Alabama woman accused of using Meta smart glasses to secretly record witnesses in a federal drug trial has pleaded guilty.

Tierra Shatalia Douglas, 36, on Thursday admitted to conspiracy to retaliate against a witness in the January prosecution of Glennie "Little Man" McGee and his wife, Echandza Maxie, according to local outlet AL.

The couple, along with Maxie’s sister, Exavieria Maxie, were involved in a multimillion-dollar drug trafficking organization that distributed bulk cocaine and fentanyl and used children as couriers, according to the Justice Department.

DRUG RING BUSTED, ILLEGAL ALIENS CUFFED BY HOMELAND SECURITY TASK FORCE IN SOUTH CAROLINA: DOJ

In the eight months following the prosecution, Douglas repeatedly harassed the witnesses and attempted to obtain their personal information before her arrest in September.

"Douglas disseminated the videos to publicly identify and intimidate the witnesses," court records said, according to AL.

The harassment included secretly recording witnesses as they left the courthouse after testifying, according to Fox10TV.

On Jan. 16, one of the witnesses said he received a video from a friend showing him exiting the courtroom after testifying, the outlet reported.

'SEE A TRUE HOLOCAUST': RELIGION PROFESSOR INDICTED AFTER ANONYMOUS ANTISEMITIC POSTS EXPOSED

In one of the videos she recorded of a witness, Douglas asked someone whether they recognized him, saying, "This guy telling, do anyone know him, he needs to be hurt," according to AL.

She also used ChatGPT to generate and distribute a flyer identifying one of the witnesses as a "snitch," the outlet said.

Reports added that Douglas sent Discord messages identifying one of the witness's minor children and the school the child attended.

In one case, Douglas allegedly sent text messages to a witness she had saved in her phone contacts as "The Rat," taunting him repeatedly for testifying.

Douglas reportedly confessed after officials confronted her with evidence that included internal surveillance footage from the courthouse.

Douglas was arrested in September and pleaded guilty Thursday.

Her sentencing is set for February 2027, according to reports.

She faces a maximum sentence of life in prison, though prosecutors reportedly agreed to recommend leniency, reports say.

item.title: New drug combo shrinks tumors in most patients facing aggressive cancer type
item.description: The pancreatic cancer pill daraxonrasib shrank tumors in 60.7% of patients when paired with chemotherapy, and 8.2% saw tumors vanish on scans.
item.content:encoded:
Pairing an experimental pill with standard chemotherapy shrank tumors or halted growth in most patients with advanced pancreatic cancer, according to early clinical trial results presented Friday at a major international cancer conference.

The findings, shared at the EORTC-NCI-AACR Symposium in Barcelona, come from a phase ½ trial testing a daily oral medication called daraxonrasib, along with two standard intravenous chemotherapy drugs, gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel.

The trial focused on 61 patients whose pancreatic cancer had already spread to other organs and who had not yet received treatment for their advanced disease.

PANCREATIC CANCER PATIENT BEN SASSE SEES 'MASSIVE' TUMOR REDUCTION WITH EXPERIMENTAL NEW DRUG

Pancreatic cancer is notoriously difficult to treat because more than half of patients are diagnosed after the disease has already spread, research shows.

In major clinical trials for metastatic pancreatic cancer, chemotherapy alone shrinks tumors in about 23% to 42% of patients, but the disease typically begins growing again after five to six months, and most patients survive between 8 and 11 months.

According to National Cancer Institute data, only about 3% of patients with distant-stage disease live five years past diagnosis.

In the new study, which tracked patients for a median follow-up of 18 months, tumors shrank in 60.7% of cases, including 8.2% where they disappeared entirely on scans. Overall, the combination stopped tumor growth in 90.2% of participants.

FDA APPROVES ONCE-DAILY PILL FOR DEADLY CANCER AFTER PATIENTS' SURVIVAL RATES NEARLY DOUBLE

Patients went a median of 12.8 months before their cancer worsened, almost double the timeframe typically seen with standard chemotherapy, and 76.6% were still alive at the one-year mark, the study found.

"We are now seeing not only substantial tumor shrinkages, including complete responses, but also durable disease control, with median progression-free survival exceeding one year," study lead Dr. Wungki Park, a gastrointestinal medical oncologist at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York, said in a press release.

More than 90% of pancreatic cancers are driven by a faulty gene called RAS, which allows tumors to keep growing. Daraxonrasib is designed to turn off that growth signal, something scientists long thought was impossible to fix with medication.

Dr. Elena Garralda, chair of the symposium and co-director of the clinical research program at the Vall d’Hebron Institute of Oncology in Spain, who was not involved in the research, said the results show that RAS-targeted drugs can be combined with existing treatments at the start of treatment to potentially achieve longer-lasting benefits.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Side effects included rash, diarrhea, fatigue and low blood cell counts linked to chemotherapy, most of which were manageable with standard care.

Only 5% of patients stopped treatment because of side effects tied to daraxonrasib.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Researchers emphasized that the findings carry some limitations.

Because this was an early-phase, single-group study involving 61 people, all participants received the experimental combination. Without a direct comparison group of patients receiving standard chemotherapy alone, doctors cannot yet confirm how much better the new regimen performs or whether it definitively extends overall survival.

The findings also apply strictly to metastatic pancreatic cancer, even though RAS mutations drive several other cancers, including certain lung, colorectal and gynecological cancers. Separate studies would be needed to test whether the combination works in those diseases.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

The trial was funded by Revolution Medicines, the California-based developer of daraxonrasib.

To determine whether these early findings translate into a durable survival benefit, researchers have launched a larger, randomized Phase 3 trial, called RASolute-303, which directly compares daraxonrasib — both on its own and combined with chemotherapy — against standard chemotherapy alone.

item.title: 'Enough': Protesters decry antisemitism after Hunter College student event including Jewish group is canceled
item.description: Pro-Israel rally organizers at Hunter College say the cancelled Cultural Arts Night shows antisemitism at CUNY, as counter protesters chant nearby.
item.content:encoded:
A crowd gathered Thursday outside Hunter College to protest after the school's student government seemingly canceled an event due to the participation of a Jewish organization.

On one side of the street, pro-Israel protesters chanted "enough is enough" and waved American and Israeli flags as speakers addressed the crowd. Across the street, a group of counter-protesters gathered waving Palestinian flags while yelling chants of their own. 

Passersby also shouted, some in support and others yelling "Free Palestine" and "F--- Israel."

JEWISH CAMPUS LIFE AT A ‘CROSSING POINT’ AS STUDENTS WEIGH ANTISEMITISM RISKS, NEW REPORT SHOWS

Organizers behind the Stand with Jewish Students at Hunter rally included the Israeli American Council (IAC), Students Supporting Israel (SSI) and #EndJewHatred. 

On flyers advertising the rally, they criticized the college's administration for not doing enough in response to what they saw as an act of antisemitism.

"We're saying enough to the marginalization of the Jewish community. We're saying enough is enough to discrimination against Jewish students. And we're saying enough is enough to this obsessive hatred of all of the symbols of Jewish life, whether it's Hillel on campus or the State of Israel," IAC CEO Elan Carr told Fox News Digital, referring to a chapter of the Jewish student group. 

Michelle Ahdoot, director of programming and strategy at #EndJewHatred, told Fox News Digital the cancellation of the event demonstrated a problem that went beyond Hunter College.

"When a multicultural event is canceled simply because Jewish students are included, we have a serious problem that goes far beyond one event at Hunter College," Ahdoot said. "The very purpose of multiculturalism is to celebrate diversity and inclusion, not to allow certain groups to decide who is welcome and who is not. 

"Any student organization has the right to choose not to participate," he continued. "But when an elected student government responds by canceling the entire event rather than standing up for the inclusion of Jewish students, it sends a dangerous message that Jewish participation is somehow unacceptable."

The Cultural Arts Night was scheduled to take place Nov. 16 but was canceled just days before. Hunter College Undergraduate Student Government (USG) flyers promoting the event showed that clubs involved included Students for Justice in Palestine, the Peruvian Student Association, Hunter Chinese Student & Scholar Association, the Taiwanese Student Association and Hunter Hillel, according to screenshots posted online.

Hillel International is a Jewish organization that can be found on college campuses across the globe. It describes itself as "a space for all kinds of Jewish students — a place where they feel welcomed and included." While its vision includes helping students make "an enduring commitment to Jewish life, learning and Israel," it is focused on Jewish life and culture, hosting holidays and holding events.

FIRE ALARM DISRUPTS NORTHWESTERN 'OCTOBER 7' PLAY BASED ON MASSACRE SURVIVOR TESTIMONY

Rita Levine Rabin Hillel at Hunter College said in a statement on Instagram it was "looking forward" to the event and that it "had no role in the decision to cancel."

"Antisemitism has no place at Hunter College. Jewish students should never be singled out, scapegoated, or made to feel unwelcome because of who they are and the anti-Semitic response online to the cancellation notice has been egregious and inappropriate," the statement read.

Ilya Bratman, who serves as executive director at Hillel at Baruch College in New York City, said the cancellation of Cultural Arts Night was a clear case of antisemitism and a sign that things could escalate.

"This is so obvious, and antisemitism has nothing to do with Israel. And that's what the main thing you have to say very loudly. This is about Jew hatred and exclusion," Bratman told Fox News Digital. "It's the first step in the process, which begins with physical exclusion of Jewish students from campuses. 

"And that is what happened in the 1930s. We know this. This is a slower process here in American campuses, and I believe this is going to keep going if we don't step up in a very serious way to stop it."

Hunter College USG announced the cancellation on Nov. 14 in a statement from Hunter College USG President Sumaiya Ahmed and Vice President Ahmad Waraich. The two student leaders claimed that "lapses in communication kept the details of this event from reaching the people at the top."

"We hear what the student body has said, and we have made the decision to cancel the event as it doesn’t align with our values or the values of the students we represent as the Hunter Community. We apologize to the clubs and students who were affected by this instance," a statement posted on Instagram read.

After the announcement, speculation about the reason for the event's cancellation grew, with some pointing to pressure from anti-Israel activists who objected to Hillel's involvement. While this was not directly addressed, Hunter USG appeared to deny it in a subsequent statement in which it said that the event was canceled over "safety concerns."

BIPARTISAN DUO LAUNCHES CONGRESSIONAL CAUCUS TO CONFRONT ANTISEMITISM AT COLLEGES

Hunter College is a public institution in the City University of New York (CUNY) system, making allegations of discrimination particularly serious since public schools are legally barred from discriminating based on religion or national origin.

Hunter College told Fox News Digital it was "deeply troubled by reports that some student groups pulled from the event because of Hillel’s participation" and said it was investigating the issue.

"There is no place for discrimination and harassment in our college community. We have policies in place to safeguard that principle and will not hesitate to enforce them," the college said in a statement provided to Fox News Digital.

Michal Mari, who is president of SSI at Hunter College, told Fox News Digital during the rally that the environment at the school has been "tough" for Jewish students. She said Jewish students had seen calls for violence against their community, including statements calling to "bring the war home" and "globalize the intifada." 

Mari believes the cancellation came after clubs dropped out of the event due to Hillel's participation, which she said was "blatant discrimination against Jewish students on campus."

"I've had professors turn their backs to me while I was speaking to them because they found out that I was wearing a Star of David or that I've been to Israel," Mari told Fox News Digital. "So, it's certainly not the most divided, but it's a place where there's work to be done."

Mari addressed the crowd at Thursday night's rally along with a number of other pro-Israel and Jewish speakers, including Shai Davidai, Ari Ackerman, Shabbos Kestenbaum and Rami Matan Even-Esh (also known as Kosha Dillz), among others, including Hunter College students.

Jayne Zirkle, who serves as director of communications for #EndJewHatred, said the organization was "incredibly proud" of the students who chose to speak publicly despite the pressures they face on campus.

"Their courage matters, and they deserve to know they are not standing alone," Zirkle said.

Davidai, a former Columbia University professor, told Fox News Digital he attended the rally to bring attention to what he saw as the "symptom" of a bigger issue.

"The symptom of canceling an event because a Jewish organization is part of it, that is a problem. And, by the way, it's a problem not just for Jews, it's a problem for everyone. Because when you cancel an event, everyone, Jewish or non-Jews, don't get to go to that event," Davidai said.

LEO TERRELL TAKES TRUMP ADMINISTRATION'S ANTISEMITISM FIGHT NATIONWIDE ON 15-CITY TOUR

While Davidai focused on the broader cultural fallout on campus, Kestenbaum, a former Harvard Divinity School student who sued Harvard over campus antisemitism, framed the issue around civil rights law and public funding.

"You cannot violate civil rights law. Colleges don't get to pick and choose which statute of the Civil Rights Act they want to subscribe to. There is one standard for all universities across the country, and if those universities insist on discriminating against students because of their ethnicity or because of their religious identity, that is illegal," Kestenbaum told Fox News Digital.

Kestenbaum is not the only one who has brought up the possible legal issues with canceling the event. New York City Council Member Eric Dinowitz publicly called for a civil rights investigation.

"[Hunter College] USG cancels a multicultural arts event because it did not align with its 'values.' It appears to be yet another chapter in the troubling history of antisemitism at CUNY and Hunter," Dinowitz wrote on X. "That's why [CUNY] must immediately launch a Title VI investigation."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Along with calls for institutional and legal accountability, speakers at Thursday night's rally encouraged students at Hunter College not to retreat from campus life and stay silent.

"Every student at Hunter or anywhere else, if you speak up, and when you speak up, we've got your back," Davidai said in an interview with Fox News Digital. 

"We've got your back with numbers. We've got your back with legal support. We got your back on social media. We have got your backs. But it's up to you to speak up, because if you don't speak up then, you know, the word doesn't come out."

Mari echoed the message, saying that the Jewish community at Hunter College was ready to rally behind those who choose to speak out.

"Courage isn't lack of fear but acting in the face of fear," Mari told Fox News Digital. "You have a community behind you. The Jewish community, especially, is one that is always behind you."

Hunter USG and Hunter Hillel did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment.
